Heart Failure

congestion and perfusion · echocardiographic phenotype · foundational therapy · diuresis and monitoring

1Illness script
Bottom line
  • Congestion or poor perfusion suggests heart failure (HF); confirm cardiac dysfunction with echocardiography. A preserved ejection fraction does not exclude HF.
  • Symptomatic chronic HF with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF): use the four foundational drug classes; add a loop diuretic for congestion. HF with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) and hypertension: control the pressure.
  • Match the intervention to the outcome: blood pressure control for uncontrolled hypertension; statins for atherosclerotic risk, rather than as HF treatment.
What it is

Inadequate cardiac performance with congestion, reduced tissue perfusion, or both.

Driver

Systolic failure: impaired contractility; diastolic failure: impaired filling of a stiff ventricle.

Triggers

Ischemia or a dilated ventricle; chronic uncontrolled hypertension is the leading cause of preserved-fraction HF.

Chain

Reduced kidney perfusion activates the renin-angiotensin system; retained fluid worsens congestion.

Insights

Orthopnea and waking breathless at night suggest left-sided congestion.

Raised jugular venous pressure and dependent edema suggest systemic venous congestion.

Afterload and ventricular remodelingA mechanism behind pressure-driven decompensation
Left ventricleUncontrolled pressure raises afterload and ventricular wall stress.Remodeling can contribute to pump dysfunction and admission.

PatternDecides itNext best step

5Diagnostic criteria
Ejection fraction
CategoryDefinition
Reduced-fraction HFLVEF 40% or less.

Preserved-fraction HFIn a patient with clinical HF: LVEF 50% or more and evidence of increased left ventricular filling pressures.

Clinical assessment
AssessMeaning
CongestionGuides diuresis.

7Treatment
1

FoundationalStable reduced-fraction HF

Use an angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI); an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB) is an alternative when appropriate.

Use an evidence-based beta-blocker: carvedilol, metoprolol succinate or bisoprolol.

Add a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (MRA) when appropriate.

For symptomatic chronic HFrEF, add a sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitor.

2

CongestionFluid retention

Add a loop diuretic and monitor kidney function and electrolytes. Titrate to relief of congestion.

3

Persistent symptomsHFrEF despite the foundational regimen

Digoxin may improve symptoms and reduce HF admissions, without a proven survival advantage.

4

Preserved fractionHypertension or volume overload

Treat hypertension and congestion; SGLT2 inhibitors may reduce HF admissions.

5

AvoidDecompensation or hyperkalemia

Start a beta-blocker after stabilization, rather than during active congestion. Avoid use of a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID), which can worsen fluid retention. Avoid excess potassium when potassium is elevated; do not intensify potassium-raising drugs before evaluation.

8Follow-up
Monitoring
WhenDo
During drug titrationRecheck renal function and electrolytes after dose increases; reassess congestion and blood pressure.
At homeCheck morning weight; seek care for continued weight gain or worsening symptoms. Avoid excessive dietary sodium; individualize the restriction.
Scenario bank
  1. 68 yo M with HFrEF, BP 168/96; which intervention most reduces hospitalization → Blood pressure control
  2. 68 yo M with HFrEF; the question asks what reduces mortality → Guideline-directed therapy – ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor
  3. 68 yo M with established HFrEF and low-density lipoprotein 150, no clinical atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) → Statin per ASCVD risk assessment → statins are neither contraindicated in HF nor beneficial for HF outcomes; the indication is atherosclerotic risk
  4. 68 yo M with HFrEF who has been advised to follow a 500 mg sodium diet → Avoid excessive sodium; individualize restriction → Dietary advice supports volume control; an extreme fixed target is not a substitute for HF treatment.
  5. 68 yo M with HFrEF on an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor, potassium 5.8 → Obtain ECG; stop excess potassium; verify a possibly spurious result
  6. 68 yo M with HFpEF and uncontrolled hypertension → Blood pressure control → the primary lever in HFpEF
Transferable rule When several values are abnormal, target the one mechanistically linked to the outcome, not the most abnormal number. Match time-to-benefit to the outcome's time horizon.
